title: Mali Gaura

lines: A POSTCARD, NOT A FAILED LETTER.
A SHORT SECTION, ITS OWN HEADING.
cards: A postcard holds a few lines and a stamp. Nobody calls it a failed letter. Sometimes it's the thing that stays on the fridge for years, because it said one thing and said it well.
Past Nat Narain in the Guru Granth Sahib, you come to a section with a postcard's size and its own full heading: Mali Gaura. It's short. It's complete.
And it has a guest at the end.

teach.h: ITS OWN NAME, ITS OWN INVOCATION.
teach.b: First, Mali Gaura gets the same treatment as the long ragas: its own name at the top and an invocation of the One, Ik Onkar, Satgur Prasad, the One Creator, known by the Guru's grace. A short raga isn't an appendix.
In the Granth, a few pages can be a whole room.

Inside, the voices are Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, and then, closing the section, Bhagat Namdev, a devotee whose hymns the Gurus gathered into the Granth beside their own. His verse is for tomorrow. Today, the opening.

Guru Ram Das begins, in plain English, not word for word, with a picture of seekers: adepts, searchers and silent sages, all turning their minds toward the Lord with longing. It's a wide view for a small room.

People known for hard practices are shown with the same longing anyone can have, and the hymn's answer is that the Guru shows them the unseen Lord. That's the sweetness of a short raga. No time to wander.
It names the longing, points to the answer, and stops.
Length isn't the measure here; a short shabad sung with attention is a complete offering. Mali Gaura says what it came to say, then hands the last word to a guest.
That's today's line: short and sweet.

how: Each raga section of the Guru Granth Sahib is sung in its own raga in kirtan; shorter sections like Mali Gaura are drawn on just as the longer ones are, and a single shabad is a complete offering in a gurdwara program.

o: a long raga sung at the close of every service
a single hymn by Namdev set to an evening tune
a short raga section, complete with its own heading

games.q: what's inside the raga — tap the pairs.

s: a short raga in the Granth is treated as an appendix
Mali Gaura has its own name and its own invocation of the One, like a full section.
Mali Gaura holds a Bhagat's hymns as well as the Gurus'
Bhagat Namdev's verse closes the section.
in Sikh practice, a longer prayer always counts for more
length isn't the measure; a short shabad sung with attention is complete.

games.q: you're compiling a scripture and a raga only has a few pages of hymns. what do you do with it?
o: fold it into a bigger raga.
give it its own heading and invocation.
leave it out as too small.
games.why: the Granth gives Mali Gaura its own name and the invocation of the One at its head. a few pages can be a whole room.

practice: Choose one short word to stay with: if you pray, Waheguru; if you don't, simply the word here. Say it once, silently, and let it be complete, without stacking more words behind it.
When the mind starts writing a longer letter, set the pen down and come back to the postcard: one word, one breath, each time enough on its own.
